description:
🚀 Meet Team LunaShift! 🌕

We're a team of passionate space explorers competing in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026!

Our project, Lunar Landing Site Navigator, uses NASA datasets to evaluate potential Moon landing sites through interactive visualization and scientific analysis.

We're looking for developers, engineers, designers, and scientists who enjoy tackling exciting challenges.

All skill levels are welcome! Join us, and let's explore the Moon together! 🚀🌕
summary:
Luna Shift is an interactive platform for comparing lunar landing sites and dates near the Moon’s south pole. It uses NASA-based terrain data and Sun and Earth position data to show the local landscape, terrain horizon, sunlight, Earth visibility, and possible communication periods.

Users can see how the selected location, date, terrain, and solar-panel direction affect power generation, battery level, science activities, and data transmission. The Planner checks whether a mission can keep enough battery power, complete its task, and send the required data to Earth before a deadline. If a landing is delayed or a location no longer works, Luna Shift compares other tested sites and dates and clearly explains why an alternative may be better.

The platform makes complex lunar conditions easier to understand through clear visuals, 3D views, and simple explanations. This is important because even a small change in location or landing time can strongly affect sunlight, communication, and mission success.
details:
Luna Shift is an interactive lunar mission-planning platform designed to make landing-site and date selection near the Moon’s south pole easier to understand. It combines NASA-derived terrain data with Sun and Earth position data to show how local hills, crater rims, and the horizon affect sunlight, solar-power generation, Earth visibility, and possible communication periods.

The platform allows users to explore a landing site in synchronized 3D views, watch a lander arrive and operate on the surface, and follow a complete mission sequence. It calculates how much electrical power the solar panels can generate, how much energy the lander consumes, how the battery charges or discharges, when a science activity can be completed, and when the resulting data can be transmitted to Earth. If the original landing date or location becomes unsuitable, the Planner evaluates tested alternatives and explains which requirements pass or fail and why.

Luna Shift is intended to bridge the gap between powerful but complex lunar-analysis tools and the needs of mission planners, educators, students, and the public. Its main benefit is that it connects terrain geometry to real operational consequences instead of only showing raw Sun and Earth coordinates. Users can see how a small change in site, date, panel orientation, or equipment height can affect mission feasibility.

Our team designed and developed the main concept, mathematical workflow, interface structure, front end, back end, 3D experience, mission logic, data visualizations, and user interaction. We built the platform using React, TypeScript, JavaScript, Three.js, Vite, Node.js, and Express, together with prepared NASA-based terrain and ephemeris data.

We also used development-support tools during our workflow, including Google AI Studio/Antigravity and model assistants such as Gemini, Hydrion, Argon, Opus 5.5, and Astra. These tools helped with brainstorming, coding suggestions, debugging, and workflow speed. However, the platform is not built around generated answers. The scientific calculations, mission checks, visual design, and final decisions are controlled by our own code and models. The optional Luna assistant only helps users navigate the platform and understand calculated results; the core planner works independently.

Our team considered scientific transparency, usability, terrain uncertainty, power consumption, communication geometry, accessibility, visual clarity, and the limitations of a prototype that is not intended for flight certification.
